task: Write one sentence of your own using the word copious. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know copious should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The bride's father shed copious tears before the vows even began — the ushers went through three packets of tissues keeping him presentable.
A sufficient supply covers the need exactly and stops there; copious sails past the need without slowing.
Plentiful already means more than enough; copious goes a rung further — abundance you measure in armloads and refills.
Overflowing outdoes even copious: a copious harvest fills every crate, while an overflowing one spills out of them onto the porch boards.

Ample means more than enough, with comfortable room to spare — ample legroom, ample time to make the train. It is a quiet measure of adequacy. Copious is louder: quantity that pours forth in armloads, arriving faster than the moment can use it.

Bountiful is abundance with a giver behind it — harvests, gifts, a grandmother's table — plenty that feels bestowed. Copious drops the giver and keeps the quantity: notes, tears, or rain simply pour forth in bulk, with no suggestion that anyone is being generous.

Copious is the right word because the sentence is about sheer pouring quantity.
'A good crop' states a fact; a copious one arrives in armloads, more than anyone quite knows what to do with.
The word's Latin root is copia, 'plenty' — copious things come in plenty, not in portions.
Copious is the abundance word for quantities that pour forth — notes, tears, rain, harvests.

Its unit-mates each stake different ground: replete describes the well-stocked container ('a shelf replete with trophies'), voluminous measures sheer bulk and volume, and prodigious adds a gasp at astonishing size.
When the point is simply 'a great deal of it, and more coming,' copious is the word.
